title: Neutropenic Fever: Infection Can Become Sepsis Fast
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Fever or new infection symptoms during significant neutropenia require immediate escalation because patients may deteriorate with few localizing signs.
recognize: Fever, chills, rigors, new cough, dysuria, line-site change, oral lesions, diarrhea, or sudden weakness may be the only clues.
priorities: Notify the oncology/RN/provider pathway immediately and obtain ordered cultures/labs without delaying urgent treatment.
assessMonitor: Trend temperature, BP/HR, mental status, oxygenation, line/wound sites, CBC/ANC, renal function, and lactate as ordered.
interventions: Use meticulous infection-control precautions and rapid sepsis workflow when indicated.
medicationSafety: Do not delay prescribed empiric antimicrobial therapy while waiting for all culture results.
teaching: Patients should know exactly which fever or infection symptoms require urgent contact based on their oncology plan.
delegationScope: Temperature collection may be delegated; interpretation and escalation require licensed judgment.
examTrap: Waiting for obvious pus or leukocytosis before escalating.
oneLinePearl: Neutropenia can hide infection signs, not infection severity.

title: Tumor Lysis Syndrome: Electrolytes Can Turn Lethal
bottomLine: After treatment of high-burden malignancy, abrupt electrolyte and uric-acid changes can cause arrhythmias, seizures, and kidney injury. Escalate new weakness, cramps, oliguria, confusion, or dysrhythmia promptly.
recognize: High tumor burden and treatment initiation increase risk.
priorities: Monitor ordered electrolytes/renal function and report rapid changes immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend potassium, phosphorus, calcium, uric acid, creatinine, urine output, ECG, and neurologic status as ordered.
interventions: Maintain ordered hydration/monitoring and prepare for urgent treatment escalation.
medicationSafety: Do not independently alter prophylactic urate-lowering or electrolyte therapy.
teaching: Report reduced urine output, palpitations, severe weakness, or confusion during early treatment.
delegationScope: I&O may be delegated; interpretation of laboratory/ECG deterioration requires licensed oversight.
examTrap: Treating new muscle cramps as benign chemotherapy fatigue.
oneLinePearl: Tumor lysis is an electrolyte emergency after cancer cells break down.

title: Malignant Spinal Cord Compression: New Weakness Is an Emergency
bottomLine: New severe back pain with weakness, numbness, gait change, or bowel/bladder dysfunction in a patient with cancer requires immediate escalation for possible spinal cord compression.
recognize: Progressive nocturnal back pain, radicular symptoms, new leg weakness, sensory change, urinary retention, or incontinence are concerning.
priorities: Protect mobility/fall safety and notify the oncology/emergency team immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend strength, sensation, gait, pain, bladder/bowel function, and neurologic changes.
interventions: Avoid unnecessary ambulation in unstable neurologic decline and prepare for urgent imaging/treatment.
medicationSafety: Administer ordered analgesia/steroids as directed; do not delay escalation while treating pain alone.
teaching: Cancer patients should report new severe back pain or neurologic changes urgently.
delegationScope: Mobility assistance may be delegated; neurologic change interpretation requires licensed assessment/escalation.
examTrap: Giving PRN analgesic and reassessing hours later despite new weakness.
oneLinePearl: Cancer plus new back pain and weakness equals cord-compression emergency.

title: Superior Vena Cava Syndrome: Facial Swelling Can Signal Obstruction
bottomLine: New facial/neck swelling, venous distention, dyspnea, cough, or positional symptoms in a patient with thoracic malignancy can signal SVC obstruction and requires rapid evaluation.
recognize: Facial plethora, upper-extremity edema, distended neck/chest veins, dyspnea, headache, or worse symptoms lying flat are clues.
priorities: Elevate the head as tolerated, assess airway/breathing, and escalate promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend respiratory status, oxygenation, edema, neurologic symptoms, and hemodynamics.
interventions: Prepare for imaging and oncology intervention; avoid unnecessary upper-extremity constriction.
medicationSafety: Do not independently start diuretics or steroids without the treatment plan.
teaching: Report rapidly increasing facial/neck swelling or breathing difficulty immediately.
delegationScope: Basic observations may be delegated; airway/neurologic deterioration requires licensed escalation.
examTrap: Treating upper-body edema as simple fluid retention.
oneLinePearl: Upper-body swelling plus thoracic cancer can mean venous obstruction.

title: Cancer-Related Hypercalcemia: Confusion and Constipation Can Be Dangerous
bottomLine: Cancer-associated hypercalcemia can present with weakness, constipation, polyuria, dehydration, confusion, or arrhythmia and needs prompt laboratory review and treatment.
recognize: Progressive lethargy, nausea, constipation, thirst, polyuria, or confusion may precede severe neurologic/cardiac effects.
priorities: Assess hydration, mental status, ECG symptoms, and report concerning changes.
assessMonitor: Trend calcium, renal function, I&O, neurologic status, and ECG as ordered.
interventions: Support ordered hydration and safety measures.
medicationSafety: Avoid independently adding calcium/vitamin D supplements when hypercalcemia is suspected.
teaching: Report worsening confusion, severe weakness, or persistent constipation/polyuria.
delegationScope: I&O may be delegated; interpretation requires licensed judgment.
examTrap: Assuming constipation is only opioid-related without considering metabolic causes.
oneLinePearl: In cancer care, constipation plus confusion may be calcium—not just medication.

title: Mucositis: Mouth Injury Can Threaten Hydration and Infection Control
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Painful oral mucositis can reduce intake, increase infection risk, and complicate medication administration. Protect the mucosa and escalate inability to drink or signs of infection.
recognize: Erythema, ulcers, bleeding, odynophagia, dry mouth, or reduced intake are key cues.
priorities: Assess oral cavity, pain, intake, swallowing, hydration, and fever.
assessMonitor: Trend oral lesions, weight, intake, hydration, and infection signs.
interventions: Use prescribed bland oral-care regimen, soft toothbrush when appropriate, and avoid irritating products.
medicationSafety: Topical/systemic analgesics require safe administration and swallowing assessment.
teaching: Use gentle oral care and report worsening ulcers or inability to maintain intake.
delegationScope: Routine oral care may be delegated; worsening mucositis requires licensed review.
examTrap: Using alcohol-based mouthwash on severely inflamed mucosa.
oneLinePearl: Mucositis is not cosmetic when intake and infection risk are affected.

title: Cancer-Related Thrombocytopenia: Prevent Bleeding Before It Starts
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Low platelets increase bleeding risk. New petechiae, bruising, mucosal bleeding, hematuria, melena, or neurologic symptoms require escalation according to severity and the treatment plan.
recognize: Bleeding can be spontaneous or triggered by trauma/procedures.
priorities: Use bleeding precautions and report active bleeding or concerning neurologic symptoms.
assessMonitor: Trend platelet count, skin/mucosa, urine/stool, menstrual bleeding, headaches, and neurologic status.
interventions: Avoid unnecessary invasive procedures and protect from injury.
medicationSafety: Review drugs that increase bleeding risk; do not independently stop prescribed anticoagulants or antiplatelets.
teaching: Use a soft toothbrush and avoid trauma; report bleeding promptly.
delegationScope: Routine observation may be delegated; bleeding assessment/escalation requires licensed oversight.
examTrap: Using IM injections routinely in marked thrombocytopenia without checking the plan.
oneLinePearl: Low platelets turn small trauma into a bigger risk.

title: Vesicant Extravasation: Stop the Infusion and Escalate
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Pain, burning, swelling, resistance, or loss of blood return during vesicant infusion can signal extravasation. Stop the infusion immediately and follow the drug-specific extravasation protocol.
recognize: Symptoms may be subtle early and vary by drug.
priorities: Stop infusion, leave access in place if protocol requires aspiration/antidote, notify the qualified oncology team, and follow agent-specific measures.
assessMonitor: Document site appearance, symptoms, drug/concentration, estimated exposure, and progression.
interventions: Use protocol-specified aspiration, antidote, elevation, and temperature measures only for the specific agent.
medicationSafety: Never flush a suspected vesicant extravasation unless the agent-specific protocol directs it.
teaching: Patients should report burning or pain immediately during infusion.
delegationScope: Chemotherapy/vesicant administration authority varies; suspected extravasation requires qualified oncology oversight.
examTrap: Flushing the line to clear the drug after infiltration is suspected.
oneLinePearl: Suspected vesicant extravasation: stop first, protocol next.

title: Cancer Pain: Reassess Function, Sedation, and Breakthrough Pattern
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Cancer pain management requires repeated reassessment of relief, function, sedation, constipation, and breakthrough frequency—not just a pain-score number.
recognize: Frequent breakthrough pain, new focal pain, escalating dose needs, or new neurologic symptoms may signal disease change.
priorities: Reassess after intervention and escalate uncontrolled or qualitatively new pain.
assessMonitor: Trend pain characteristics, sedation, respiratory status, function, bowel pattern, and adverse effects.
interventions: Use ordered pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic comfort measures.
medicationSafety: Monitor opioid-related sedation/respiratory depression and bowel effects; do not independently escalate dose.
teaching: Use the prescribed breakthrough plan and report major changes in pattern or function.
delegationScope: Pain scores may be collected by trained staff; interpretation and medication response require licensed review.
examTrap: Documenting a lower score without checking sedation or function.
oneLinePearl: Pain relief is only safe when function and sedation are reassessed too.

title: Malignant Pericardial Effusion: Watch for Tamponade Physiology
bottomLine: Cancer-related pericardial effusion can progress to tamponade. New dyspnea, tachycardia, chest pressure, hypotension, distended neck veins, or worsening weakness requires urgent escalation.
recognize: Symptoms may progress from exertional dyspnea to hemodynamic compromise.
priorities: Assess ABCs, vital signs, mental status, and notify the emergency/oncology team immediately when tamponade is suspected.
assessMonitor: Trend BP/HR, oxygenation, chest symptoms, neck veins, perfusion, and mental status.
interventions: Prepare for urgent diagnostic and drainage intervention as ordered.
medicationSafety: Do not treat unexplained hypotension with routine medications without evaluating the underlying cause.
teaching: Report rapidly worsening dyspnea, chest pressure, or fainting urgently.
delegationScope: Vital-sign collection may be delegated; tamponade recognition/escalation requires licensed judgment.
examTrap: Assuming dyspnea is only anemia or deconditioning in a cancer patient with hypotension.
oneLinePearl: Effusion becomes an emergency when it impairs filling and perfusion.
